summary: Summarizes the 2012 IAB/IRTF workshop in Vancouver on congestion control for interactive real-time communication and lists recommendations for the IETF. The views are those of participants.

eli5.summary: Experts met to talk about how video calls can avoid clogging the internet. This is the report of what they said.

questions: congestion control for real-time communication workshop
how should video calls handle network congestion
how does tcp friendly rate control work
why is rtcp feedback too slow
subtitle: Report on congestion control mechanisms for real-time video and voice calls.

tldr.problem: Interactive real-time communication like video calls creates significant internet traffic, but many applications do not implement proper congestion control, risking network overload and unfair competition with other traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB and IRTF workshop in Vancouver examined technical approaches and network infrastructure improvements needed to implement effective congestion control for RTP-based video and voice calls.
tldr.outcome: The workshop recommended network infrastructure changes and application-level techniques to avoid self-inflicted queuing, leading to the formation of the RMCAT working group to standardize algorithms.

today: RFC 7295 is an Informational document reporting on a July 2012 workshop. The RMCAT working group it spawned has since standardized congestion control algorithms such as NADA, SCREAM, and Google Congestion Control (GCC). Deployment of ECN and modern AQM algorithms in routers remains limited, though data center networks increasingly use both.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
The internet carries many types of traffic, and since 1988 it has mostly remained stable because applications like email and file transfers use the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), which automatically reduces transmission rates when the network becomes congested. However, real-time interactive applications such as voice and video calls typically use UDP with the Real-Time Transport Protocol (RTP), often with no congestion control or only basic mechanisms.

As web-based video communication (including WebRTC) grows rapidly, the lack of robust congestion control in these applications threatens the internet with potential overload. Unlike file transfer, video calls need very low delays and cannot buffer extensively, creating a different set of engineering challenges. The workshop sought to address how to implement congestion control that works well for real-time applications while remaining fair to other traffic.
sections.eli5: Right now, video calls and web pages can fight over internet bandwidth, but video calls don't have good rules for sharing like file downloads do. As more people use video calls, we need to make them play fair.

sections.title: Challenges of Real-Time Congestion Control
sections.content:
Real-time media faces unique constraints that differ from traditional bulk data transfer. The codec (the software that encodes audio or video) can only change its output rate in coarse steps, not smoothly. Audio typically sends one packet every 20 milliseconds, and video sends 25-30 frames per second—timing constraints that TCP does not consider. Feedback about network problems arrives slowly in RTP via the RTP Control Protocol (RTCP), much less frequently than TCP acknowledgments.

Measurements from real networks showed that video applications struggle with TCP traffic. When one TCP connection runs alongside a voice call, the voice quality degrades at startup. Six concurrent TCP flows can destroy audio quality entirely. Additionally, excess buffering in routers—a problem called bufferbloat—masks congestion by delaying packets rather than dropping them, making it harder for applications to detect when the network is overloaded.

Attempts like TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) aim to match TCP's throughput while providing smoother transmission, but TFRC assumes the network controls the codec, whereas modern video codecs generate variable-bitrate streams based on content. This mismatch complicates deployment.
sections.eli5: Video calls need to send at certain rates and times, unlike files that can wait. Routers get too full and delay packets instead of dropping them, so video apps can't tell when the network is congested. Making video and files share fairly is hard.

sections.title: Workshop Recommendations
sections.content:
Participants recommended a two-pronged approach. First, network infrastructure should be upgraded: routers should separate queues for different traffic types so real-time flows do not fill buffers meant for bulk data. Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) allows routers to signal congestion early before packets are dropped, giving applications time to reduce their rate. Active Queue Management (AQM) algorithms like CoDel prevent queues from growing too large. These technologies already exist but are not widely deployed.

Second, applications should implement congestion managers—code within the browser or application that coordinates multiple flows (audio, video, data) and reacts to all available congestion signals, including packet loss, delay increases, and ECN marks. Applications should avoid sending large bursts at startup and instead probe the network carefully. The simplest approach targets self-inflicted queuing—preventing one application's multiple flows from blocking each other.

The workshop acknowledged that network upgrades take time and that applications must work reasonably well even on unupgraded networks. Both paths can proceed in parallel. The work led to the creation of the RMCAT (RTP Media Congestion Avoidance Techniques) working group to standardize algorithms and the AQM working group to improve router infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Routers need to handle video and files separately, and video apps need to ask the network politely about congestion rather than just blasting data. Both changes can happen at the same time, and most of the technology already exists.

sections.title: Deployment Challenges
sections.content:
A key tension emerged during the workshop: should congestion control be in charge of the codec, or should the codec be in charge and adapt only when necessary? Congestion control prefers steady, managed rates but risks latency if it backs off too conservatively. Codecs prefer to send at their natural rate for quality but can create sudden bursts. TCP itself has been questioned—some participants argued that changing how TCP is used in browsers (avoiding excessive parallel connections, as HTTP/2 does) might accomplish more than redesigning congestion control.

Participants also debated whether the problem was primarily at the protocol level or required application-layer coordination. One consensus emerged: no single congestion control algorithm is perfect, and algorithms must be tested extensively with real-world network conditions, not just simulations. The path forward requires interaction between the network layer (providing signals), the transport layer (implementing algorithms), and the application layer (managing user experience).
sections.eli5: Nobody completely agreed on the best way forward, but everyone agreed we need real-world testing, not just lab tests, and we need different parts of the system to work together instead of independently.
